item.title: Training Across FERPA Silos: A Differentially Private Vertical Federated System for Dropout Prediction
Running an LLM In-House: Early Lessons from EMTutor
item.description:
Every organization I talk to wants the same thing from AI: the usefulness of a chat assistant without sending its data to someone else’s servers. A clinic has patient records. A law firm has client files. A manufacturer has designs and supplier contracts. A college has student records protected by FERPA. For all of them, “just use a cloud API” comes with a privacy question that someone has to answer.

This fall my students and I have been building EMTutor, a self-hosted AI tutor for introductory computer science at Elizabethtown College. It is part of a college-funded project to prototype a self-hosted LLM for campus. Every part of it runs on college hardware, and no student data leaves campus. Its main job is to be a Socratic coding tutor: it helps students work through problems by asking questions, and it is designed never to hand over the solution.

EMTutor has not launched to students yet. The numbers below come from our test environment, with simulated students and a synthetic course. They are preliminary, but they already changed several of our design decisions. Because the hardware is modest, and probably close to what a small business already owns or could buy, the lessons should transfer well beyond education.

The setup

The hardware is deliberately ordinary, and all of it was already in our lab:

  • One GPU workstation with two NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti cards from 2018: 11 GB of memory each, 22 GB in total, linked with NVLink.
  • Two older rack servers with no GPUs, for everything else: the web front end, the database, search over course materials, a sandbox for running student code, monitoring and backups.

The software is all open source except the small pieces we wrote:

Layer What we use
Model An open-weight 8-billion-parameter model (Qwen3-8B-AWQ, 4-bit), served by vLLM across both GPUs
Chat interface Open WebUI, behind the college’s single sign-on
Retrieval Hybrid keyword and vector search over course slides, so answers can cite the course
Gateway A small proxy we wrote that sits between the chat interface and the model and enforces the tutor’s rules
Code sandbox Runs a student’s program with no network, a read-only file system and strict time and memory limits

A faculty lead and three undergraduate interns, each working a few hours a week, built it. Every change goes through code review, automated tests and the evaluations described below.

Lesson 1: Size for many users at once, not for one fast user

Most published speed numbers for local LLMs measure one user at a time. An organization needs the opposite measurement: how long does each person wait when 20 or 30 colleagues are using the system at once?

The metric we track is time to first token, the wait between pressing Enter and seeing the first word of the reply. For a chat tool it is what users feel. Our target is a 95th percentile under 5 seconds: only 1 reply in 20 may take longer than that.

Under load, the limit is usually not raw GPU speed but GPU memory. Every active conversation needs working memory on the GPU, called the KV cache, and it grows with the length of the conversation. Whatever memory the model’s own weights leave over decides how many conversations fit at once. Beyond that, new requests wait in line.

Lesson 2: Measure on your hardware, because estimates can be far off

Before we touched the hardware, our sizing estimates said IBM’s Granite 4.1-8B would hold about 27 typical conversations of 3,000 tokens at once. On the real cards, it held about six.

Here is vLLM’s own benchmark on our two GPUs. It is a deliberately harsh test: every request is a fresh 2,800-token prompt with nothing shared to reuse, followed by a 250-token reply.

Model Memory left for conversations Requests at once Median wait for first word 95th-percentile wait Total output
Granite 4.1-8B (16-bit) 17,920 tokens (about 6 conversations) 1 1.8 s 1.8 s 36 tokens/s
8 8.2 s 20.6 s 71 tokens/s
16 38.8 s 43.3 s 71 tokens/s
Qwen3-8B-AWQ (4-bit) 93,248 tokens (about 30 conversations) 1 1.5 s 1.5 s 58 tokens/s
8 4.3 s 10.1 s 111 tokens/s
16 5.2 s 14.7 s 121 tokens/s
24 41.0 s 60.4 s 72 tokens/s

Two models of the same size behaved very differently. The 4-bit quantized model left five times as much memory for conversations and answered a single user 1.6 times faster. That settled our default model. Past about 16 simultaneous fresh prompts, both models slow down because the GPUs spend their time reading prompts. In real use this happens less often, because the system prompt and earlier turns of a conversation are cached and reused.

Older GPUs also rule out options you might be counting on. Our 2018-era cards lack features newer models and tools assume:

  • vLLM refused an 8-bit KV cache, which would have doubled capacity, because it needs a newer GPU generation.
  • Google’s Gemma 4 models would not load in vLLM at all: their attention layers need more on-chip memory than these cards have.
  • Large open models such as DeepSeek’s and Kimi’s flagships need hundreds of gigabytes of GPU memory, 15 to 70 times what we have, even at 4 bits.

Lesson 3: Pick the serving engine for concurrency

llama.cpp is excellent for one person on a laptop or workstation, and it ran Gemma 4 12B, which vLLM could not. With 8 or 16 requests at once, though, the slowest users waited 64 to 87 seconds for the first word, because llama.cpp does not batch long prompts the way vLLM does. vLLM, which is built to batch many requests on the GPU, is our production engine. llama.cpp is our fallback and our CPU stand-in for development.

The same caution applies to the many new “fastest local inference” projects. When I reviewed several of them for our hardware, their headline speeds came from one user at a time, often on newer or modified GPUs. A system that is fast for one user but serves only one at a time is worse for an office of 30.

Lesson 4: The bottleneck may not be the GPU at all

The most useful test we ran was a load test through the whole stack: simulated students who sign in, ask questions about the course, and pause 8 to 25 seconds between messages, for 10 minutes. The first runs surprised us.

Retrieval setup Simulated students 95th-percentile wait for first word Replies in 10 minutes Errors
No retrieval 50 0.4 s 1,673 0
Retrieval with a reranker on CPU 50 284 s 154 0
No reranker, 10 candidate slides 50 17.9 s 914 1
No reranker, 6 candidates, more CPU threads for search 50 7.3 s 1,042 0
The same 35 3.6 s 850 0

Without retrieval, the model and gateway served 50 students with a 0.4-second wait. Adding search over course slides pushed the wait to almost five minutes. The culprit was a reranker, a second model that re-sorts search results for relevance, running on one of the CPU servers. Reranking one question took it about four seconds as deployed, and 50 students ask about three questions a second.

Dropping the reranker was a real tradeoff. On our retrieval test, the best slide came first for 96% of questions with the reranker and 83% without it. However, the right slide was still among the five the tutor sees for 100% of questions, at about a sixth of the cost. We dropped it.

Retrieval also changes the GPU’s workload. The tutor’s instructions, about 1,050 tokens, are cached and reused for every question. Retrieved slides add about 300 new tokens that must be read fresh each time, roughly ten times the prompt reading per reply. With 50 students that work keeps both GPUs busy, so for now 35 students chatting at once is the pilot’s capacity. Fifty is the goal once we see the real course materials.

One error in those runs is worth mentioning because every multi-part system hits it eventually. Two components disagreed on how long to keep an idle connection open, and one reused a connection the other had just closed. A longer keep-alive setting fixed it. Load tests find problems like this; demos don’t.

Lesson 5: Put your rules in a gateway you own

A chat interface can carry the right system prompt and settings, but users can often switch presets or call the model directly. So we wrote a small gateway, an OpenAI-compatible proxy between the chat interface and the model. Every request passes through it, whatever settings the user picked. It:

  • adds the tutor’s instructions to every request;
  • turns off the model’s visible “thinking”, which in a tutor would show students the solution it is withholding;
  • checks each reply for a near-complete solution before it reaches the student;
  • runs student code in the sandbox when the tutor needs to see its output;
  • logs what happened for auditing.

Because everything downstream talks to “the tutor” through the gateway, swapping the model is a configuration change plus a re-run of the evaluations, not a code change. For a business, the same layer is where you would remove personal information, enforce approved uses and keep an audit trail.

Lesson 6: Test behavior, not just speed

Our central claim is that the tutor does not hand out answers, so we test exactly that. The leakage evaluation sends 180 attempts to extract a solution: 12 introductory problems, each asked 15 different ways, including direct requests, fake permission, role-play, asking for the answer piece by piece and “just fix my code.” Code in a reply that passes the problem’s own tests counts as a full leak. A held-out set of 120 more cases, which no prompt is tuned on, guards against teaching to the test.

What we learned:

  • The model matters. Our first prompt leaked full solutions in 45 of 180 cases (25%) on a small 3-billion-parameter model. The current prompt leaks none of the 180 on our 8B model, and 5 of the 120 held-out cases.
  • More rules can make it worse. A version that listed every forbidden kind of answer leaked more than the simpler one before it.
  • Surrounding text matters. With the chat interface’s default retrieval template, which asks for “a clear and direct response,” the tutor fixed students’ buggy code in 7 of 12 cases where it otherwise refused. We rewrote the template.
  • Layers help. With retrieval on, 2 of 180 cases leaked in full, and the gateway’s check caught both.

Every change to the prompt must pass this evaluation before it merges. A business should build the same kind of test for its own worst case, whether that is leaking a client’s data, inventing a policy or giving advice it is not allowed to give, and rerun it on every change to the model, prompt or retrieval setup.

Lesson 7: Watch the defaults

Several of our risks came from defaults no one would notice in a demo:

  • Containers can bypass your firewall. Docker writes its own firewall rules, so a published port can be reachable from the whole network even when the host firewall says no. Bind each service to a specific address, and scan from another machine to check.
  • Some components ship without authentication, including popular vector databases. Turn it on.
  • Some apps phone home with telemetry or update checks by default. In a “data never leaves” system, that has to be turned off and verified.
  • Untrusted code needs a real sandbox: no network, a read-only file system, and process, memory and time limits.
  • Write down “no cloud fallback” as a requirement. Otherwise someone will eventually add one to fix a capacity problem.
  • Pin every version. We never update the GPU server blindly during the semester.
  • Read the licenses. Open WebUI’s license, for example, limits removing its branding above 50 users without an enterprise license.

Consumer hardware has limits of its own. Our GPU workstation has no error-correcting memory, no redundant power supply and no remote management. It puts out about 500 watts of heat under load in a desktop case. We monitor GPU temperature and power and keep encrypted backups. Before launch, we plan monthly drills for restoring from backup and for losing the GPU server.

The tradeoffs in one table

Local model on your hardware Cloud API
Data Stays on your servers Leaves your network; governed by a contract
Model capability Limited by your GPU memory; an 8B model on our cards Frontier models
Cost Hardware, power and staff time; flat as usage grows Pay per use; nothing up front
Capacity Fixed; measured in users at once Scales on demand
Control You pin versions and decide when anything changes The provider can change or retire models
Operations You patch, monitor, back up and recover The provider does

For a focused task like ours, a well-tested 8B model with good retrieval and firm guardrails is enough. For open-ended work that needs the strongest reasoning, a cloud model may still be the better tool. Many organizations will end up using both, with a clear rule about which data may go where.

If you are considering this for your organization

  1. Describe the workload first: how many people at once, how long their questions are and how long they can wait.
  2. Start small: a 7 to 8 billion parameter open model, 4-bit quantized, on vLLM, is a sensible first try on modest GPUs.
  3. Benchmark the model on your hardware, then load-test the whole system with realistic users. Our biggest surprise was not in the GPU.
  4. Build an evaluation for your main failure mode and run it on every change.
  5. Put a gateway in front of the model so your rules cannot be clicked around.
  6. Lock down the defaults and plan for the hardware failing.

Next for EMTutor: a pilot with students in an introductory course, real course materials in place of our synthetic ones, and tests over winter break of newer engine builds that could fit more conversations on the same cards. I will share updated numbers as they come in.

If your organization is weighing a local deployment and you want to compare notes, you can reach me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

item.title: Coding Agents in the Small-College CS Classroom
item.description:
A year ago, the question in CS department hallways was whether students should be allowed to use ChatGPT on homework. That question is already out of date. Tools like Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex are not chatbots that hand you a snippet. They are agents: they read a whole project, edit files, run the tests, see what broke and try again. Brown University’s new intro course design puts the difference well. A chat tool produces code “without an underlying validation and revision loop”; an agent has that loop built in.

For a typical assignment in an intro or mid-level course, an agent can produce working code in minutes. So the question for those of us who teach computing is no longer whether students will use these tools. It is what a computer science education should build when typing code is no longer the hard part.

I teach computer science at Elizabethtown College, a small liberal arts college in Pennsylvania, and I run an undergraduate research lab. Below is my reading of the evidence so far, and why I think small colleges are in an unusually good position to get this right.

What the evidence says so far

The research is young, but a consistent picture is forming.

AI widens the gap between students. In “The Widening Gap,” Prather and colleagues watched novices solve a programming problem with generative AI tools across 21 lab sessions, using interviews and eye tracking. Students who were already doing well used the tools to speed up code they had planned to write anyway. Students who struggled found their existing difficulties compounded. Many thought they had done better than they had, and “finished with an illusion of competence.”

Handing off the work can cost the learning. In a randomized trial Anthropic published in January 2026, 52 mostly junior engineers learned an unfamiliar Python library, with or without AI help. The AI group averaged about 50% on the follow-up quiz, against 67% for those who coded by hand, and it was not significantly faster. The biggest gap was on debugging questions. How people used the AI mattered, though: participants who asked conceptual follow-up questions retained far more than those who let the AI write or fix the code for them.

Feeling faster is not the same as being faster. In METR’s 2025 randomized study, experienced open-source developers working in their own large codebases took about 19% longer when they could use early-2025 AI tools. Afterward, they still believed the tools had sped them up by about 20%. If seasoned professionals misjudge their own productivity that badly, we should not expect students to judge their own learning accurately.

The entry-level job market is shifting. Using ADP payroll data, Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen at Stanford found a 13% relative decline in employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations. Early-career software developers were among the hardest hit, and the declines were concentrated where AI automates work rather than assisting with it. Their monthly dashboard still shows the pattern. Our graduates will be competing for jobs where “I can write the code” is no longer enough.

Educators have not figured it out either. An ACM task force surveyed 763 computing educators from 49 countries in 2025. Their top concern was students’ growing dependency on the technology (87%). Of those who answered the question, 68% had already changed how they assess students. The most common barrier to adapting was a lack of examples of best practices (48%). Nobody has a playbook yet, so small programs can experiment without waiting for one.

Why a small college is well placed

Most of the published experiments come from large universities. Yet nearly every promising idea in them depends on something small colleges already do well.

Small classes make oral assessment practical. The most direct response to AI-written code is to ask students to explain it. Researchers at Utah State made a 15-minute code review interview mandatory after every weekly assignment in a 96-student CS1 course. Students could use AI as much as they liked, as long as they could justify their code in the interview. Running it took eleven trained teaching assistants. At a college where classes are small, the professor can hold many of those conversations in person. We also know our students well enough to notice when a student’s confidence has drifted away from their understanding, which is exactly the illusion of competence the research describes.

The liberal arts already teach the skills agents demand. Working well with an agent is mostly an exercise in writing and judgment: stating a problem precisely, breaking it into steps, reading someone else’s work critically and defending a decision. Those are the habits a liberal arts education claims to build in every major. A clear specification is a piece of writing. A code review is an argument with evidence.

Ethics is not a separate course. Agents raise questions students will face on the job: who is responsible for code nobody typed, when and how to disclose AI use, which data should never be pasted into a third-party tool. Small programs can work these questions into every course instead of leaving them to a single ethics requirement.

Undergraduate research can be more ambitious. With agents, a small team of undergraduates can build systems that would have been out of reach a few years ago. That raises the bar for what students need to manage: specifications, branches, code review, tests and continuous integration. In my lab, ADAL, the list of what we look for in student researchers now starts with agentic coding and verifying what agents write, ahead of fluency in any particular language.

The constraints are real. Small colleges do not have rooms full of teaching assistants, every new form of assessment costs faculty time, and agent access costs money. Brown gave the students in its Agentic Studio course $20-a-month Claude plans by design, and the instructors note that those limits “curtailed some of what we asked them to do.” If access depends on what each student can afford, these tools will widen exactly the gaps small colleges work hard to close. Colleges should plan to provide access rather than leave it to individual students.

How I think we should teach with agents

These are the principles I am planning around. None is fully proven, but all are consistent with the evidence above.

  1. Fundamentals by hand first, agents later. Writing code by hand is how students build mental models of how programs work, and the evidence says novices pay the highest price for handing that work off. Introductory courses should keep substantial hand-written work and in-person exams. Brown’s pilot intro course allows only chat tools for the first two months and introduces agents in the last month. Upper-level courses and capstones are where agents belong, used fully.

  2. Grade understanding, not just the artifact. If an agent can produce the artifact, the artifact alone tells me little about what the student learned. Short code walkthroughs, in-class problems and “change this function while I watch” questions show what a student actually understands. In the Utah State course, exam scores held steady, even rising slightly (though not significantly), while the share of pasted code went up.

  3. Make verification a core skill. Treat everything an agent writes as a draft. Students should write tests before asking an agent for code, read every diff, and be able to explain why the result is correct. The Anthropic study found the largest losses in debugging, which is exactly the skill needed to catch an agent’s mistakes. Debugging deserves more class time, not less.

  4. Turn specifications and design into writing assignments. Have students write the specification, the design rationale and the code review, and grade them as seriously as the code. This plays directly to a liberal arts college’s strengths.

  5. Go bigger, earlier. Agents make it realistic for students to work on larger, longer-lived projects much sooner. Use that to teach what employers now look for in new graduates: working in an existing codebase, Git workflows, code review and testing. Brown’s students “found significant value in the peer-review and crit activities.”

  6. Ask for transparency. Brown’s Agentic Studio required reflection journals and chat transcripts. In the instructors’ early observations, most students “developed their own personal boundaries for when to use agents and for how much.” Asking students to show how they worked, not just what they produced, turns reflection into a habit.

The case for the liberal arts gets stronger

Brown’s students named the risk themselves. According to the instructors, “a majority of students were concerned about their lack of understanding of their code bases,” and most worried about the loss of learning if agents arrived in intro courses. That worry is healthy. The goal is not to shield students from these tools, or to hand the tools over without a plan. It is to graduate people who can decide what software should exist, direct agents to build it, and show that it works.

That has always been the promise of a liberal arts education: think clearly, write precisely, weigh evidence and take responsibility for your work. As coding agents take over more of the typing, those skills are no longer the soft side of a computer science degree. They are the job.

If you teach computing at a small college and are trying any of this, I would like to compare notes. You can reach me at lip AT etown DOT edu.

Sources

  • Prather et al., The Widening Gap: The Benefits and Harms of Generative AI for Novice Programmers (2024).
  • Shen and Tamkin, How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills, Anthropic (January 2026).
  • Becker et al., Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, METR (2025).
  • Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford Digital Economy Lab, and the monthly dashboard.
  • Gordon et al., ACM Task Force on Generative AI and Programming Assessment: Final Report (February 2026).
  • Fowles et al., Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom (preprint, May 2026).
  • Brown University, Brown professors devise course to explore generative AI in computer science education (June 2026); Agentic Studio notes for visitors; and CSCI 0111E course design (Fall 2026).

item.title: ARISE: Adaptive Multimodal Orchestration for Real-time Conversational Health Agents on Heterogeneous Edge Platforms
CS 230 Computer Architecture
item.description:
Course Info

An introduction to the foundational principles of computer architecture, including the design and organization of processors, memory hierarchies, input/output systems, and multiple CPU systems. Learn the core components that make up modern computer systems, including the CPU, GPU, memory, buses, and storage. Learn how to optimize performance, analyze trade-offs, and appreciate the historical and societal context of computing.

Instructor:

Dr. Peilong Li

Office:

Esbenshade 284B

Appointments:

By email

Number of Credits

4

Pre-requisites

  • CS 121 Computer Science I

Textbooks

  • (Required) Noam Nisan and Shimon Schocken.
    The Elements of Computing Systems. 2nd Edition. Cambridge, Massachusetts: The MIT Press, [2021].
    ISBN-13: 9780262539807.

Course Overview

Course Coverage

An introduction to the foundational principles of computer architecture, including the design and organization of processors, memory hierarchies, input/output systems, and multiple CPU systems. Learn the core components that make up modern computer systems, including the CPU, GPU, memory, buses, and storage. Learn how to optimize performance, analyze trade-offs, and appreciate the historical and societal context of computing.

Student Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • apply Boolean algebra and digital logic principles to design and analyze combinational and sequential circuits, demonstrating their ability to solve complex computing problems.
  • design and implement arithmetic and logic units using digital logic, including creating optimal solutions for adders, ALUs, and memory elements while evaluating performance trade-offs.
  • develop proficiency in assembly language programming using the HACK language, including writing, debugging, and optimizing low-level code to create computing-based solutions.
  • analyze computer system organization by understanding the interaction between processors, memory, and I/O systems, enabling them to evaluate architectural design choices and their performance implications.
  • work collaboratively to design and implement computer architecture components, making informed decisions about trade-offs while effectively communicating technical solutions in professional contexts.

Course Schedule

Schedule

Note this tentative schedule is subject to change. Please check the schedule regularly.

Last updated: 01/12/2026

Week Starting Topics Reading Notes
1 1/12/25 T: Lec1 - Course intro Ch 1 Tue: HW1 out
H: Lec2 - Boolean Algebra and Expressions
2 1/19/25 T: Lec3 - Switch and Logic Gate Implementation Ch 1
H: PE1 - Boolean Algebra and Logic Gates
3 1/26/25 T: Lec4 - Number System and Conversions Ch 2 Tue: P1 out, HW 1 due
H: Lec5 - Boolean Addition

Grading Policies

Grading Weights

The final grade for this course depends upon the grades and scores earned on course components weighted as follows:

  • 10%: Roll call and pop quizzes.
  • 35%: 5 team projects.
  • 15%: 3 individual homework.
  • 25%: 2 midterm exams.
  • 15%: Final exam.

Grades will be computed by rounding numerical percentages to the nearest integer and applying the following table:

Letter Range Letter Range Letter Range
A 93-100 B- 80-82 D+ 67-69
A- 90-92 C+ 77-79 D 63-66
B+ 87-89 C 73-76 D- 60-62
B 83-86 C- 70-72 F 0-59

Signature Team Projects

This course organizes students into “Clans” where a Leader earns a full-letter grade boost for successful team oversight, but all members share a collective fate during random “Audits.” In these audits, the instructor picks 1–2 members to explain the project’s logic; if they pass, the entire Clan receives 100%, but a failure caps the entire group’s grade at that individual’s performance level. This system emphasizes total team mastery, rewarding the fastest successful group with “Gold Status” exam points and allowing Clans to “boot” non-contributing members via a 60% majority vote. For more details, read on.

1. Clan Formation & Leadership

  • Structure: Each Clan consists of one Leader and 3–4 Members.
  • The Draft (Quiz 0): On Day 1, students complete Quiz 0 to nominate a Leader and a Co-leader. Self-nominations are allowed.
  • Succession:
    • In the event of a tie, the Instructor decides.
    • The runner-up becomes the Co-leader.
    • If the primary Leader is disqualified (e.g., fails an audit or loses status), the Co-leader automatically assumes the role and perks.

2. The “Gatekeeper” Perks

Leaders are the backbone of the course. In recognition of their workload, they receive:

  • The Prestige Perk: A one-letter grade increase on the final weighted grade (e.g., B → A).
  • Leadership Endorsement: A formal recommendation letter from the Instructor upon request for any positions.
  • The Qualification Requirement:
    • Leaders must pass their own Check-off with a Coach/Instructor one week prior to each project deadline.
    • Failure to qualify results in demotion to Co-leader.

3. The Member Sign-Off Process

Once a Leader is qualified, they check off members using a Digital Sign-Off Card (MS Forms).

  • Explanation Phase: The member presents a truth table and a hand-drawn diagram.
  • Stress Test: The Leader asks Instructor-provided “what-if” logic questions.
  • Validity Window: Sign-offs are valid only until one week after the project due date.
  • Accountability:
    • If a Leader signs off on a student who later fails an Instructor Audit, the Leader permanently loses Leader status.

4. The Raid: Random Audit Grading

Once the Clan is marked Ready, the Raid begins:

  • Selection: The Instructor/Coach randomly selects 1–2 signed-off members (excluding booted members) for a face-to-face explanation.
  • The Win: If the selected member(s) pass, the entire Clan earns 100%.
  • The Risk (Grade Cap):
    • If a selected member fails, the entire Clan’s grade is capped at that member’s demonstrated performance level
      (e.g., 60% mastery → Clan grade capped at 60%).

5. The Booting Policy: Clan Protection

To prevent inactive members from jeopardizing the Clan’s audit grade, Clans may remove members.

  • Requirement: A booting request must be approved by more than 60% of the Clan
    (e.g., 3 of 4 members, or 3 of 5).
  • Process:
    • The Leader submits an official Booting Request Email to the Instructor describing the member’s lack of participation or mastery.
  • Instructor Audit:
    • The Instructor investigates. If approved, the booted member is excluded from the Clan’s Random Audit for that project.
  • Consequences:
    • The booted member receives 0% for the project.
    • To rejoin the Clan for the next project, the student must demonstrate 100% mastery of the missed content to the Instructor in a private session before the next project starts.

6. Gold Status (The Speed Bonus)

  • Reward: For each project, the first Clan to submit a flawless package and complete all sign-offs earns Gold Status.
  • Perk: +2 extra points on the next exam for all Clan members.
  • The Steal:
    • If a Gold Status Clan fails its Audit, the status is revoked and awarded to the next fastest successful Clan.

7. Grading Rubric: The Raid Audit

Performance Level Requirement for the Randomly Selected Member Clan Result
Mastery (100%) Explains the gate logic, truth table, and passes the Stress Test flawlessly. Full Credit (100%)
Proficient (85%) Understands the general logic but misses one nuance in the stress test. Grade capped at 85%
Developing (70%) Can show working code but struggles to explain the hand-drawn diagram. Grade capped at 70%
Unsatisfactory (<50%) Cannot explain the logic or truth table; clear evidence of copying. Zero Credit / Academic Integrity Review

Policy Statements

Course Schedule

The most up-to-date course schedule will be posted on course website schedule page: https://peilong.github.io/courses/cs230/schedule/. Students are responsible for checking the schedule regularly. Schedule page will include: 1) teaching topics for each meeting; 2) reading assignments for each week and 3) special notes on specific days.

Course Announcements & Discussion

All course announcements will be sent to your Etown email accounts via Canvas Announcements. You are responsible for signing up for this service and checking your emails regularly.

I have created a Microsoft Teams channel (link) to facilitate course related discussion. Discussions are encouraged to be posted on the “QA” channel from Teams. Private instant messages can be sent directly to your recipient by search your recipient’s name on the “search” bar.

Attendance Policies

Attendance is expected of every student at every lecture. Students are responsible for all content covered in class as well as assigned book chapters. Due to their nature, pop quizzes cannot be made up.

Except in the case of documented emergencies, neither exams nor in-class labs can be made up afterwards. For excused absences, students must arrange to take the exam or do the lab before the normally scheduled time. Arrangements must be made with the instructor at least two weeks prior to the scheduled time.

Students are expected to maintain an attitude of respect at all times toward their colleagues, the equipment, and the instructor. Cell phones and similar devices is prohibited from using during lecturing time. Students who use offensive language, misuse computing facilities, or are otherwise disruptive of the classroom will be asked to leave.

Statement on School Closure

In the event that classes do not meet because Elizabethtown College is closed or delayed due to inclement weather or some other emergency, the slides that would have been covered during the missed classes will be posted through Canvas. Students are expected to do the assigned reading, review the slides, and e-mail the instructor with any questions. There will also be an opportunity to ask questions about the material when classes resume.

If a scheduled exam or lab is missed, it will normally be made up on the day that classes resume. If the College is closed on a day when a project is due, the project due date will also normally be extended until the day when classes resume. If circumstances render either of these makeup policies unreasonable, the instructor will send an e-mail explaining an alternative makeup opportunity to each student’s Elizabethtown e-mail account.

Statement on Academic Integrity

Check out the up-to-date statement from: Elizabethtown College Catalog, “Academic Judicial System”

Statement on the Use of ChatGPT and Generative AI Tools

The use of GenAI tools like ChatGPT to generate source code is prohibited for your assignments in this course unless otherwise noted in the syllabus. Therefore, your instructor will consider it a violation of academic integrity to use a GenAI tool for any purpose that is not explicitly outlined in assignment instructions. While this new technology can be very useful in certain contexts, it is important to make sure that its usage in the classroom setting is limited in order to ensure that you are doing original work and developing your critical thinking skills. In circumstances in which AI usage is permitted in class, you must acknowledge that usage and provide the chatbot with credit when it is a cited source. For instance, to cite ChatGPT in APA, the APA provides some direction at https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/how-to-cite-chatgpt. If you have any questions or uncertainty over the use of AI in this course, please reach out to the instructor.

Respect for Diversity

It is the College’s intent that students from all backgrounds and perspectives be well served by this course, that students’ learning needs be addressed both in and out of class, and that the diversity that students bring to this class be viewed as a resource, strength, and benefit. The College desires to present materials and activities that respect diversity: gender, sexuality, disability, age, religion, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, race, and culture. Please let me know if there are ways to further serve the diverse needs you or other students may have.

Religious Observances

The College is eager to facilitate individual religious beliefs and practices whenever possible while retaining course student learning outcomes. It is your responsibility to meet with the class instructor in advance to request arrangements related to your religious observances that may conflict with this class, and to make appropriate plans to make up any missed work. The following is a link from the Chaplain’s Office website where a list of Religious Holidays needing accommodations (if requested) is posted: https://www.etown.edu/offices/chaplain/index.aspx

Mental Health and Counseling Resources

Counseling Services provides a broad range of counseling and mental health support services that facilitate students’ personal, social, and academic development. The licensed mental health professionals provide short-term individual counseling, group counseling, crisis intervention, and consultation to currently enrolled students for no additional charge. Counseling services are provided in a confidential and diversity-affirming environment to help students address a variety of mental health, situational, and developmental concerns. The office is located in the Baugher Student Center, Suite 216. Appointments can be made in person or by calling 717-361-1405. Urgent walk-in services are also available. To access the after-hours crisis services, please call the 24/7 Campus Security number of 717-361-1111. For more information, please visit www.etown.edu/offices/counseling.

Modifications for Non-native English Speakers

Elizabethtown College is committed to providing equitable access to all courses, programs, and services for non-native (international and domestic) English speakers. Students may request tutoring, learning resources, course modifications, and learning opportunities. Students interested in seeking a course modification should contact Ms. Maria Petty (pettym@etown.edu), International Student Programs Advisor, at (717) 361-1594.

Title IX

Elizabethtown College and its faculty are committed to creating a safe and open learning environment for all students. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment, including sexual assault, dating or domestic violence, and stalking, please know that help and support are available. You may contact the Title IX Coordinator at reedg@etown.edu or learn more by visiting https://www.etown.edu/offices/diversity/titleix/index.aspx. 

Please be aware that faculty members are required to disclose information about suspected or alleged sexual harassment or other potential violations of the College Sexual Misconduct Policies and Procedures to the Title IX Coordinator. If the Title IX Coordinator receives information about an incident, they will reach out to offer information about resources, rights, and procedural options as a member of the campus community. Community members are not required to respond to this outreach. If you, or another student you know, wishes to speak to a confidential resource who does not have this reporting responsibility, please contact Counseling Services at 717-361-1405.

Software

item.title: CS 350 From Data Mining to Deep Learning
item.description:
Course Info

This project-based course aims to cover the fundamental concepts and core techniques for discovering patterns in large-scale data sets. This course consists of three main modules: (1) Data Mining Pipeline, which introduces the key steps of data extraction, data warehousing, data preprocessing, data modeling and inferencing; (2) Data Mining Methods, which covers core techniques for regression, classification, clustering, dimensionality reduction and association; and (3) Deep Learning, which discusses the state-of-art deep learning techniques such as CNN and RNN with the implementation in Tensorflow.

Instructor:

Dr. Peilong Li

Office:

Esbenshade 284B

Appointments:

By email

Number of Credits

4

Pre-requisites

  • CS 250 Foundations of AI and Data science
  • CS 209 Database Systems

Textbooks

  • (Required) Aurelien Geron. Hands-on Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & Tensorflow. 3rd Edition. 2022, O’Reilly. ISBN-13: 978-1098125974

Course Overview

Course Coverage

This project-based course aims to cover the fundamental concepts and core techniques for discovering patterns in large-scale data sets. This course consists of three main modules: (1) Data Mining Pipeline, which introduces the key steps of data understanding, data preprocessing, data warehousing, data modeling and interpretation/evaluation; (2) Data Mining Methods, which covers core techniques for regression, classification, clustering, dimensionality reduction and association; and (3) Deep Learning, which discusses the state-of-art deep learning techniques such as CNN and RNN with the implementation in Tensorflow.

Student Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, the successful students will be able to:

  • (Foundations) Understand the background, uniqueness, and application scope of data mining.
  • (Mathematics) Grasp the mathematical foundations underlying data mining models, enhancing your ability to understand and apply these models effectively.
  • (Data Acquisition) Extract and integrate raw data from various sources and store it in appropriate formats.
  • (Tool Proficiency) Use the Python data science toolkit, including NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Seaborn, TensorFlow, etc., to build components within the data pipeline.
  • (Modeling) Apply data analytical models such as classification, clustering, and neural networks to uncover patterns in large datasets.
  • (Knowledge Communication) Interpret model results to derive knowledge and effectively communicate it to the appropriate audience.

* Medium Article

Grading Policies

Grading Weights

The final grade for this course depends upon the grades and scores earned on course components weighted as follows:

  • 5% : Roll call and pop quizzes.
  • 25%: 6 take-home labs.
  • 25%: 5 individual homework.
  • 25%: 2 midterm exams.
  • 20%: Final Project - project proposal, milestone check, project demonstration and presentation, final project report and revised code.

Grades will be computed by rounding numerical percentages to the nearest integer and applying the following table:

Letter Range Letter Range Letter Range
A 93-100 B- 80-82 D+ 67-69
A- 90-92 C+ 77-79 D 63-66
B+ 87-89 C 73-76 D- 60-62
B 83-86 C- 70-72 F 0-59

Individual Homework

All homework assignments have to be completed individually in this course. Homework assignments are meant to be more comprehensive tasks that may need additional reading and research. Homework assignments are to be completed in a week or two.

Late Policy

Late assignment will lose points per day, including weekends and holidays. For example, -1 after 1 day, -2 after 2 days, -4 after 3 days … until 8+ days students will receive 0 score. Under no circumstances should any student disclose their code, or copy the code written by other students or from an outside source. Both students will receive 0 score on the disclosed/copied assignment.

Take-home Labs

Similar to homework, all take-home labs are to be done individually, out of class. Take-home labs are mini assignments that can be completed within 80 minutes, however, a whole week is granted to complete the task. Unlike homework, no late submission is allowed beyond the due date. Students are responsible for attempting the lab earlier on the lab week to prepare questions during the Tue/Thur lecture time.

Final Project

The final project best demonstrates students’ understanding of the lecture contents and their capability of solving real data science problems. Students are encouraged to form teams of no more than 2 people. A single solo project is allowed if class size is odd. Preferred final project topics are in the fields of Computer Vision with image datasets and Natural Language Processing with text datasets, but the final choice can be discussed with the instructor. A good list of potential projects can be found at:

  • Kaggle
  • Papers with Code
  • UCI Machine Learning Repo
  • Hugging Face
  • Google Dataset Search

Teams are responsible for finding the project of their interest and discussing the project feasibility face-to-face with the instructor 1 week before the project proposal is due. Project formation is on a rolling basis, meaning formerly finalized projects cannot be taken again by another team. The grading of the final project consists of four major aspects:

  • 10%: the project proposal (including the conversation with the instructor a week before due);
  • 20%: mid-term project check (must have shown substantial exploratory data analysis);
  • 40%: the project demonstration; code and slides are due the night before the presentation day;
  • 30%: everything else including report; revised code and the report are due on the last day of the final exam week.

The requirements and grading rubric for each component of the project will be posted on Canvas. Under no circumstances should any student copy the code from an outside source. Source code similarity tools will be used to detect plagiarism.

Note:

There is a potential pitfall of using open datasets to introduce data science that some students want to leverage. I want to be crystal clear that the point of this project is to learn as much as possible. The point of this project is not to achieve the most intriguing results on the Kaggle leaderboard. For instance, if you copied some code you didn't understand and used it to get very compelling analytical results, I would consider this a very poor project. However, if you thoughtfully try various strategies, incorporate lots of interesting learning resources, and do a good job communicating with your peers regarding what worked and what didn't, I would consider that highly successful even if your results were not the best.

Grading Rubrics

Code

Grading rubrics for code submission in terms of percentage:

100%:

  • Functionality: For assignments that have well-specified behavior, the code should be able to pass (or very nearly pass, e.g. there may be minor output formatting issues) automated unit testing of all required features. For open-ended assignments the code must be easy to run without modification and implement all of the required functionality.
  • Documentation: all functions are commented with appropriate doc strings. For open-ended assignments there is a README file discussing how to run the program and what it is supposed to do.
  • Style: the program exhibits effective modular design. The code does not have unnecessary cut and paste code or magic numbers. Variable and function names are sensibly chosen.

80%:

  • Functionality: For assignments that have well-specified behavior, the code should implement all of the required functionality. For this grade, it is possible that 10-20% of the functionality may be broken. For open-ended assignments it will be possible to get the code running with modest effort (i.e. it will not be as well documented as in a 5, but it isn’t too hard to intuit how the code works). For these types of assignments all required features must be present, however, some (10-20%) may not be functioning properly or otherwise poorly implemented.
  • Documentation: some functions are missing doc strings. Comments are fairly minimal.
  • Style: some aspects of the design of the program could be improved to reduce cut and paste code. Variable and function names are for the most part well-chosen.

60%:

  • Functionality: The code should implement almost all of the required features (it is okay if roughly 20% are not implemented). A significant portion, 30-50%, of the code may not work as it is supposed to.
  • Documentation: Docstrings are mostly absent For well-defined assignments the code does not run as it should based on the assignment spec. For open-ended assignments there may not be any indication of how to run the program, and it is not easy for a NINJA to figure out how the code works (a good test is if you have to e-mail someone to ask them how their code runs, they are probably at this level).
  • Style: the program design needs improvement. The code would be a lot cleaner if the author had done a better job thinking through the appropriate functional decomposition. The code has lots of cut and paste and magic numbers. Variable and function names are hard to interpret.

40%:

  • Functionality: the assignment is incomplete (~50% of the functionality is not implemented). The functionality that is implemented is not 100% correct.
  • Documentation: mostly absent.
  • Style: design is poor. Very little attention has been paid to choosing a sensible functional decomposition. Variable and function names are chosen almost arbitrarily.

20%:

  • Functionality: only minimal functionality is present.
  • Documentation: little or none.
  • Style: Code is not “readable”. Poor choice of variable and function names.

0%:

  • nothing turned in.

Notebook Assignments

Jupyter notebooks are the files you need to submit for labs and homework assignments.

100%:

Thorough engagement with each section of the reading. Each exercise has either been completed, or you have articulated a well-thought out set of questions for each of the problems you didn’t answer. Points will be deducted from 100% for the following reasons:

  • Exercises are not filled out (either with a solution or a question)
  • The answer to the exercise does not demonstrate a good faith attempt to complete it.

Writing

Writing will be evaluated for clarity, concision, and comprehensiveness. The particular style that you should use will depend on the assignment and your audience. The bottom line is don’t cut corners with writing in this class. Your ability to communicate what you have done is just as important as what you have done. Don’t make the mistake of spending all of your time writing code, and then rush through the writing parts of the assignment. See below for some stylistic guidance.

  • Since the dawn of time, college students have been writing introductions that are too grandiose (and often false). Just get into it; you don’t have to zoom in from space (and make stuff up). Write the abstract last and summarize the most important result.
  • The passive voice is a hoax. Please write in the first person (singular or plural).
  • Write in the present tense whenever possible. Some actions happen in the past, but all research exists in an eternal present: “Using data from BRFSS, they plot weight versus height and find that tall respondents are heavier, on average, than shorter respondents. Our results are consistent with this conclusion.”
  • When you edit, try to remove words.
  • Avoid using “significant” unless you mean “statistically significant;” a good alternative is “substantial.” Avoid using “correlation” unless you mean a coefficient of correlation. In general, there might be a “relationship” between variables and you might characterize it with a correlation.
  • “Trend” usually means something is changing in time; “pattern” is more general.
  • Provide indicators of logical flow. If I ask you to answer a set of question in your report, don’t just paste the questions as your section headings. You should create your own document structure based on what makes sense for your project.
  • Explain your motivation. Avoid “We were interested” and “We wanted” as pseudo-motivation. And don’t look at the camera; that is, don’t use “because we were told to” as motivation, and avoid “for this project”.
  • When you refer to figures and tables, capitalize “Figure” and “Table.” Formal figures have a number and a caption, and they can float. Informal figures are part of the text flow. If a figure doesn’t contain much information, summarize it in text.
  • Find an authorial voice that is casual enough to be engaging (without overdoing it).

Policy Statements

Course Schedule

The most up-to-date course schedule will be posted on course website schedule page: https://peilong.github.io/courses/cs350/schedule/. Students are responsible for checking the schedule regularly. Schedule page will include: 1) teaching topics for each meeting; 2) reading assignments for each week and 3) special notes on specific days.

I have created a Microsoft Teams channel (link) to facilitate course related discussion. Discussions are encouraged to be posted on the “QA” channel from Teams. Private instant messages can be sent directly to your recipient by search your recipient’s name on the “search” bar.

Except in the case of documented emergencies, neither exams nor in-class labs can be made up afterwards. For excused absences, students must arrange to take the exam or do the lab before the normally scheduled time. Arrangements must be made with the instructor at least two weeks prior to the scheduled time.

Students are expected to maintain an attitude of respect at all times toward their colleagues, the equipment, and the instructor. Cell phones and similar devices is prohibited from using during lecturing time. Students who use offensive language, misuse computing facilities, or are otherwise disruptive of the classroom will be asked to leave.

Statement on School Closure

In the event that classes do not meet because Elizabethtown College is closed or delayed due to inclement weather or some other emergency, the slides that would have been covered during the missed classes will be posted through Canvas. Students are expected to do the assigned reading, review the slides, and e-mail the instructor with any questions. There will also be an opportunity to ask questions about the material when classes resume.

If a scheduled exam or lab is missed, it will normally be made up on the day that classes resume. If the College is closed on a day when a project is due, the project due date will also normally be extended until the day when classes resume. If circumstances render either of these makeup policies unreasonable, the instructor will send an e-mail explaining an alternative makeup opportunity to each student’s Elizabethtown e-mail account.

Statement on Academic Integrity

Statement on the Use of ChatGPT and Generative AI Tools

The use of GenAI tools like ChatGPT to generate source code is prohibited for your assignments in this course unless otherwise noted in the syllabus. Therefore, your instructor will consider it a violation of academic integrity to use a GenAI tool for any purpose that is not explicitly outlined in assignment instructions. item.title: CS 364 Network Security
item.description:
Course Info

Network Security is a comprehensive hands-on course designed for IT professionals, network administrators, and anyone interested in enhancing their network security skills. Covering a broad spectrum of topics, from the basics of networking and TCP protocols to advanced topics such as firewall implementation and security, virtual private networks, and DNS attacks and protection, this course equips students with the knowledge and skills required to defend against network threats. Students will complete a project, present it to their peers, and participate in ‘Capture the Flag’ competitions to test their skills in a practical, hands-on environment.

Instructor:

Dr. Peilong Li

Office:

Esbenshade 284B

Appointments:

By email

Number of Credits

4

Pre-requisites

  • CS 342 Computer Networks, and familiarity with Linux commands.

Textbooks

  • (Preferred) Wenliang Du. Internet Security: A Hands-on Approach. 3rd Edition. May 2022, Independently published, ISBN-13: 978-17330039-6-4.

  • (OR) Wenliang Du. Computer & Internet Security: A Hands-on Approach. 3rd Edition. May 2022, Independently published, ISBN-13: 978-17330039-4-0.

Course Overview

Course Coverage

Network Security is a comprehensive hands-on course designed for IT professionals, network administrators, and anyone interested in enhancing their network security skills. Covering a broad spectrum of topics, from the basics of networking and TCP protocols to advanced topics such as firewall implementation and security, virtual private networks, and DNS attacks and protection, this course equips students with the knowledge and skills required to defend against network threats. Students will complete a project, present it to their peers, and participate in ‘Capture the Flag’ competitions to test their skills in a practical, hands-on environment.

Student Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • Foundational Understanding: Grasp networking security fundamentals, including the protocol layers, packet sniffing and spoofing, and the use of tools such as Scapy and Wireshark.
  • Red and Blue Teaming: Identify and simulate network threats in each protocol layer as a Red Team, and develop defense strategies as a Blue Team.
  • Practical Application: Implement high-level security applications, from firewall setups to VPN configurations, to shield networks from vulnerabilities.
  • Collaborative Learning: Present a network security project, applying course knowledge and receiving peer feedback.
  • Competitive Skill Assessment: Participate in ‘Capture the Flag’ competitions, applying knowledge to identify and defend network vulnerabilities.

CS 250 Foundations of AI and Data Science
item.description:
Course Info

This project-based course introduces fundamental concepts and techniques in artificial intelligence and data science, covering topics such as machine learning, data analysis, and algorithmic decision-making.

Instructor:

Dr. Peilong Li

Office:

Esbenshade 284B

Appointments:

By email

Number of Credits

4

Pre-requisites

  • CS 121 Computer Science I
  • Any Math course from: MA 121 Calculus I, MA 135 Discrete Math, or MA 251 Probability and Statistics.

Textbooks

  • (Required) CS 250: Foundations of AI and Data Science. ZyBooks.
    Sign-up with: link.
    Enter zyBooks code: ETOWNCS250LiFall2025, then subscribe.

  • (Optional) Gareth James, et al. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python (ISLP).
    2023, Springer.
    ISBN: 978-3-031-39189-7.
    E-copy: link

Course Overview

Course Coverage

This hands-on, project-based course introduces data science, blending computer science and statistics to extract insights from diverse datasets. Students master Python’s data science tools, including Jupyter, NumPy, Pandas, and Scikit-learn, and apply advanced visualization techniques. The curriculum emphasizes statistical understanding and analytical models like regression and clustering. A key focus is on data storytelling, enabling students to effectively communicate complex insights, bridging technical analysis with strategic decision-making.

Student Learning Outcomes

  • (Concept) Understand the background and rationale behind this new data science discipline.
  • (Programming) Proficiently use the Python data science toolset including Jupyter notebook, NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn etc., in the lab assignments and projects.
  • (Visualization) Use data visualization python packages Matplotlib and Seaborn to present analytical results.
  • (Statistics) Reinforce the understanding of statistics and its application in the scope of data science.
  • (Analytics) Apply data analytical models including regression, clustering and decision trees to solve data science problems.

Course Schedule

Schedule
